evals.prompt: Define a theme system in 2-3 sentences. Name its tiers and state which tiers components are allowed to consume.
expected_elements: A contract between design decisions and component code expressed as named tokens; appearance changes without editing components
Three tiers: reference tokens (raw values), system/semantic tokens (intent-named), component tokens (component-specific overrides)
Components consume only system and component tokens — never raw values or reference tokens
A theme provides the reference-to-system mapping; the indirection is what lets one swap repaint everything

evals.prompt: Why does a three-tier token system exist instead of a flat list of color variables? What does the indirection buy?
expected_elements: Separates three different rates of change: brand values (rare), theme assignments (occasional), components (continuous)
A flat system collapses them into one rate and forces every component to know every brand value
Each tier gives a rate of change its own surface to evolve on
Net effect: a single theme swap repaints the product; a new theme is just new system-token values

evals.prompt: Why are semantic token names (color.background.surface) preferred over descriptive names (color.gray.100), and what is the cost of the descriptive form?
expected_elements: Semantic names tell the component author what to use (intent) without knowing today's value
Descriptive names force the author to know that gray.100 happens to be the surface color today
Descriptive names leak appearance into the contract and break meaning when the theme flips
The discipline is to resist convenience names that encode appearance

evals.prompt: How are CSS custom properties used to deliver themes at runtime, and how is a single subtree given a different theme (e.g. a dark hero inside a light app)?
expected_elements: A theme is a set of custom-property assignments scoped to a selector (:root for default, [data-theme="dark"] for alternates)
Custom properties cascade and inherit, so a subtree override is a single attribute change on that subtree
Token definitions live in a single source-of-truth file (ideally DTCG JSON) generated into the CSS variable layer by a build step
Tooling (Style Dictionary, Tokens Studio, Terrazzo) transforms tokens into platform outputs

evals.prompt: What are the three operational pieces of runtime theme switching, and why is a small inline script in the document head usually needed?
expected_elements: Persistence (localStorage, or a cookie if SSR-sensitive)
Application: a class or data attribute on the document root set before first paint to avoid a flash
Propagation: notify components that read theme imperatively (chart libraries, canvases)
A small inline head script runs before the stylesheet loads so the theme attribute is set pre-paint
SSR pages serialize the chosen theme into the initial HTML so first paint matches preference

evals.prompt: A teammate asks the theme-system-design skill to pick the exact hex value for the brand's primary blue and to handle prefers-color-scheme detection. Are those in scope? Route each correctly.
expected_elements: Picking the hex / designing the palette is out of scope — that is color-system-design
prefers-color-scheme detection and OS-preference / asset variants are out of scope — that is dark-mode-implementation
theme-system-design owns the token contract, indirection layer, and runtime switching mechanism that those values plug into
Correctly distinguishes owning the contract from owning the values and the platform detection

evals.prompt: A stakeholder says 'a theme system is just a set of color variables you toggle.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: The value is the tiered indirection and semantic naming, not the variables themselves
A flat variable list with no tiers provides no separation of rates of change and no safe additive/breaking contract
Semantic intent names keep appearance out of the component contract; descriptive names break on theme flip
Components must stay off the reference layer; token rename/removal is a breaking change requiring a deprecation cycle

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a theme system is implemented correctly?
expected_elements: Components reference only system/component tokens; a grep for raw hex or reference tokens in component code returns zero matches
Runtime theme switch causes no full-page repaint flicker; the theme attribute is set before first paint
A new theme can be added by providing only new system-token values, with no component files modified
Removing/renaming a system token causes a build- or lint-time error, not a silent runtime fallback
SSR pages serialize the chosen theme into initial HTML; docs list every semantic token by intent, not appearance
